title: Chapter 50: The Roof Garden, Part 1 of 5: Oren's Page
html:
The first thing Corin did on Saturday morning was read a man his own life.
He did it before he did anything else. Before he looked at his leg. Before he looked at the children. Before he let himself think about Monday. He did it because it was written on the first page of the Ledger, in his own square capitals, in the margin, where he could not miss it: Read Oren his page every morning. Before anything. He asked.
So he did.
The side vault of the crypt of Saint Bride's was very cold at that hour. It was always cold. It was a low stone room cut off the end of the long hall, with a round ceiling like the inside of a barrel, and a stone bench along one wall where Corin slept, and above the bench a long niche in the wall full of the skulls of monks. There were thirty-one of them. Corin had counted them on his first night, when the fever was going down and he could not sleep. They sat in a row on the shelf of stone, brown and smooth and very old, with their empty eyes looking out over the room, and somebody long ago had painted a name on each forehead in faded red paint. Brother Anselm. Brother Hugh. Brother Dunstan. Most of the names had rubbed away. One skull, at the end, had no name at all, only a little painted cross.
Corin had grown fond of them. They did not talk. They did not ask him how his leg was.
The lamp was on the floor where Lyra had left it, turned down very low. There was a gray light coming in too, from a little iron grating high up in the wall at the end of the vault, where the crypt came up to the level of the graveyard outside. Through the grating Corin could see snow, and the bottom of a yew tree, and one gray stone with a name on it that he could not read from here. The snow had stopped in the night. Everything outside the grating was very still and very white.
Oren was sitting on an upturned crate by the arch.
He had been sitting there when Corin fell asleep, after midnight. He was sitting there now. Corin did not know if he had moved at all in between. He sat very straight, the way old soldiers sit, with his left arm in its black sling across his chest and his right hand on his knee, and his big gray head turned a little toward the long hall, listening. He had Terrence's old coat on, with the bald fur collar. Under the coat, Corin knew, there was a sword wrapped in sacking, and under the sacking the sword had a little dark stain near the point that Oren had not cleaned off yet, because he only had one hand and it was hard.
"Oren," said Corin quietly.
The big man turned his head.
"Morning, sir." His voice was low and rough. "All's well."
It was what he said every morning. All's well, sir. He had said it every morning for twenty-two years, Lyra had told Corin, at the foot of the stairs on Crown Walk, to Lord Thorne, before Lord Thorne went out. He had said it on the barge to an old man who only tapped. Now he said it to Corin, in a crypt, under a shelf of skulls, with his arm in a sling and half his life gone out of him. And he still meant it. Corin could hear that he meant it.
"Come and sit here," said Corin. "Where I can see you."
Oren got up. He did it carefully, because of his shoulder and because of the hurt in his side where he had fallen on the stair at Madame Hesper's. He brought the crate across and set it down by the bench and sat on it, and put his right hand on his knee again, and waited.
Corin opened the Ledger.
It was a fat black book, very battered, with HARBOUR TIDE TABLES stamped on the cover in faded gold, because Corin had bought it secondhand in Quill Row and had never had the money for a new cover. Inside, it was all his. Every page. His whole life, as far as he still had one. Names and faces and promises and debts. Lists of what he had burned and lists of what he owed. He turned the pages carefully with his gray fingers. His fingers did not bend well any more. They were stiff and dull and the color of old pewter, from the tips to past the wrists, and on a cold morning like this they hardly felt the paper at all. He had to watch them to be sure they had hold of a page.
Near the back, after his own pages, there was a page with a name at the top in big square letters.
OREN.
Corin had written it on Thursday night, in the crypt, while Oren watched. He had written it big, so that Oren could look at it. Not read it. Oren could not read it. Oren could not read anything now. But he could look at it, and know it was there.
"Ready?" said Corin.
"Ready, sir."
Corin read it to him.
He read it slowly and clearly, the way he would have read a list of names in a court. He read the top part first, which was the part about who Oren was. Oren. Forty-six. Born in the north. Learned his letters at six, in a dame school, from a woman with a cane. Joined the Commonwealth Foot at sixteen. Sergeant. Came to the Thorne house at twenty-four. Captain of the household guard. Twenty-two years. Taught Lady Lyra to ride. Taught Master Rowan to ride the gray pony, and let go of the saddle. Brother: Harlan. Mother: dead, six years. Loves: the Thornes. Hates: being thanked.
Oren's mouth moved a little at that last line. It might have been a smile.
Then Corin read the second part, which was the part he hated to read. The list under the heading SPENT.
Autumn. The arch in Wharf Street: spoon.
The Saltmarsh: the drum calls. All of them. And the drums.
The barge, against the hooks: lock. Ice. Chair.
Lilies.
Thursday. Velvet Street. Madame Hesper's shop: reading and writing. All of it.
He stopped there. There was nothing else on the list yet. He hoped there would never be anything else. He knew there would.
Oren sat very still on the crate.
He did not ask what a spoon was. He had asked, the first morning, and Corin had told him, and Oren had nodded and said right, and Corin had seen in his face that it meant nothing to him at all. The word went into him like a stone into a pond with no bottom. So now he did not ask. He just listened to the words go past, all the things he had given away to hold a wall in front of people he loved, and his big face did not change.
After a moment he said, "And the last bit, sir."
Corin turned the page.
On the next page, at the top, under the words THOSE I OWE, there was one line in Corin's hand, written on Thursday night.
Madame Hesper. Agnes. She held her door.
He read it.
Oren nodded, once. Slowly. Then he looked down at his right hand on his knee.
"Agnes," he said. "I keep that one. I don't know how. I can't read it no more. But I keep that." He turned the hand over and looked at the palm, as if the name might be written there. "Four pins in her mouth. I took them out."
"I know."
"Put them in the little red cushion. On her wrist."
"I know, Oren."
The big man was quiet. Out in the long hall, a child coughed, and then another, and then they were quiet again. Somebody was moving about by the braziers. Mrs. Doyle, by the sound of it, singing under her breath, very low, and banging a pot.
"Sir," said Oren.
"Yes?"
"The boy's shape. On the floor." He nodded at the stones by the bench without looking at them.
Corin looked down.
The four shapes were still there. In blue chalk, on the gray stone floor, where Gideon had drawn them on Thursday for a man who could not read. A boot. A fork. A gate with a belly. A tent. Big and careful and a little crooked, the way Gideon drew everything, with his tongue between his teeth. Nobody had swept them away. Mrs. Doyle swept the crypt every morning with a stiff broom, all the way along the long hall and into every vault, and she had swept round them. Corin had watched her do it, yesterday, frowning, going all the way round the four shapes with the end of her broom as if they were a sleeping cat.
"Still there," said Corin.
"Good." Oren looked at them then. He looked for a long time. "Lyra," he said.
He did not read it. He could not read it. Corin knew that. But he looked at the four blue shapes the way a man looks at a face he knows, and he said the name, and it was right.
"That's it," said Corin. His voice did something he had not meant it to.
"A boot," said Oren, very low. "A fork. A gate with a belly. A tent." He nodded. "I'll know it. If I see it. Anywhere. I'll know it."
He got up then, carefully, and took his crate back to the arch, and sat down on it again with his face to the long hall, and was a guard again.
Corin sat with the Ledger open on his knee and looked at the page for a while after that, without reading it.
Then he made himself look at his leg.
It lay out in front of him along the bench, straight, the way it would always lie now. Doctor Silas had bound it from the hip to the ankle with strips of clean linen and two long splints of ash wood, one on each side, so that it could not bend. Not that it could have bent anyway. The knee was gone. Not gone the way a memory goes, all at once, into the dark. Gone the way a door goes when somebody nails it shut. On Tuesday night, in the Bourse, on the kitchen stair, he had walked on it when Silas had told him not to, and something in the back of the knee had torn all the way through, and the joint had filled with blood. And now, Silas said, the blood would turn to bone, slowly, over the winter, and the knee would set like that. Straight. For good. He would walk with a stick in a month, if he was lucky. He would swing the leg from the hip, like a man walking on a wooden leg. He would go up stairs sideways. He would never run again. Never kneel. Never climb. Never ride a horse.
He had written it down himself on the SPENT page, on Wednesday, in his own hand. Tuesday. The Bourse. The bend in my left knee. For good. Silas told me before. I went anyway. And under it, smaller: Not a memory. Still counts.
It hurt this morning. It hurt every morning. A deep dull hot ache all along the back of the thigh, where the iron rod had gone in at Bridewell, and a hard tight swollen feeling in the knee itself, as if somebody had packed it with wet sand. He did not mind the hurt so much. The hurt was honest. It was the stiffness he minded. The way the leg lay there, along the bench, like a log somebody had put next to him. Like a part of him that had already decided to be something else.
He took a breath and let it out.
Then he looked at the other bench.
Lyra was asleep.
She was asleep on the floor, the way she had slept every night that week, on a folded blanket with her back against the cold stone wall at the end of the vault, under the grating. She had not taken off her mother's gown. She had come in after midnight in it, with Gideon and Oren, and sat down in it on the floor by his bench and told him everything that had happened in her aunt's house, every word, in order. The lilies. The cups. The nurse. The box. The pins. And then she had not got up again. She had fallen asleep where she sat, halfway through a sentence, with her head against the wall, and Corin had not woken her. He had sat and watched her sleep instead, for a long time, with the Ledger on his knee, until he slept too.
Now the gray light from the grating fell on her. On her short dark hair, cut ragged just below her ears. On the gray silk of the gown, which was creased now, and had a little dark mark on the skirt where she had knelt on the crypt floor. On her hands in her lap, still in Madame Hesper's old wedding gloves, which were pale gray kid and very thin and had a tiny pearl button at each wrist. Somebody had put Oren's coat over her in the night. No. Not Oren's. Oren's coat was on Oren. It was Gideon's coat. The thin brown jacket that Gideon wore over everything. And Gideon himself was asleep across the arch from Oren, curled up on the floor with his knees to his chin and his new brown boots still on, in his shirt.
Corin looked at the coat over her, and at the boy without it, and did not say anything.
On the floor near Lyra's hand there was a piece of paper folded small. Corin knew what it was. It was the Duke's card. His Grace the Duke of Marrow attends Councillor Thorne's Midwinter reception tonight. She had carried it all the way to her aunt's and back.
He thought about her, last night, in the white room, with a silver cup in front of her that she had not drunk from. He thought about her standing at the foot of her aunt's stairs while an Inquisitor tapped four numbers on the banister in front of her, and not answering. He thought about how she had looked when she came in under the arch. Very white. Very straight. And then her face, when she had seen him, and it had just stopped.
The bravest thing I have seen anyone do in that house in twenty years. That was what the Duke had said to her, she told him. She had said it in a flat voice, as if she did not believe it.
Corin believed it.
He closed the Ledger. He put it on the bench beside him, with his gray hand flat on the cover.
Then, inside him, very faint, so faint he was not sure for a moment that he had heard it at all, something stirred.
Not a word. Not this time. Just a stir. The way a sleeper stirs in the next room. Malakor had been nearly silent since Sunday night, since the Ash lamp by the wet door at the Bourse had burned through Corin's hands and put the old man's voice out like a candle. He had said Corin's name once, faintly, under a bridge. He had said careful once, at the arches. That was all. For six days, the voice that had lived in the back of Corin's head for as long as he could remember, dry and sharp and bossy and old, had been very nearly nothing.
Corin waited.
Nothing came.
He let out his breath.
Saturday, he thought. Two days.
And out in the long hall, by the braziers, Mrs. Doyle stopped singing, and a door banged somewhere up above, at the top of the crypt steps, and he heard the doctor's quick heavy feet on the stone coming down.
The Notice
Doctor Silas came in under the arch with snow on his shoulders and a piece of paper in his hand, and his face was the color of the paper.
He was a very tall man, and very thin, like a heron standing in a ditch, with long legs and long arms and a long narrow tired face. His spectacles sat crooked on his nose. They always sat crooked. One of the arms had been mended with black thread, and it made the left lens sit a little higher than the right, so that he always looked as if he were asking a question with one eye. He wore an old black coat that was too short in the sleeves, and under it a gray waistcoat with three buttons missing, and he smelled, as he always smelled, of wet-dog medicine and carbolic and very strong tea.
This morning he also smelled of cold. He had been outside.
He did not say good morning. He came straight across the vault to the bench and held out the paper to Corin, and his long fingers were shaking.
"It was on the door," he said. "The church door. The big one. Nailed. With four nails. A clerk did it at first light, Amos says. With two men from the Watch standing behind him while he did it, in case anybody minded." He breathed out hard through his nose. "Nobody minded. There was nobody there to mind. It's Saturday. It's snowing. I took it down."
"You took it down," said Corin.
"I took it down." Silas pushed his spectacles up his nose with one finger, which only made them more crooked. "They'll put another up. I know that. They'll have a hundred of them. I don't care. I wasn't going to leave it there for the mothers to read." He paused. "The ones who can read."
Corin took the paper.
It was a good paper. Thick and white and smooth, with a clean edge, not the gray rag paper that the parish notices were printed on. There were four little torn holes along the top where the nails had been, and the snow had made a damp gray mark across one corner. At the very top, pressed into the paper, there was a seal in blue wax. A white hand, holding up a small gold lamp. The same seal that had been on the vials in the doctor's bag in the Bourse, in the counting room, on the night Corin had taken one. He knew it the way you know a face that has hurt you.
Under the seal the words were printed in black, in neat tall letters, very clear.
BY ORDER OF THE OFFICE OF PUBLIC HEALTH
NOTICE OF REMOVAL
It being known to this Office that a number of children of the river parishes, suffering from the river fever and from the falling sickness that follows it, are at present kept without proper care in the crypt of the parish church of Saint Bride's, in conditions dangerous to their health and to the health of the city;
It is hereby ordered that the said children, to the number of fifty-one, shall be removed by the carts of this Office on MONDAY, being Midwinter Day, at the SEVENTH BELL of the morning, to the House of Rest for the Simple and the Aged, beyond the tanneries, where they will be kept warm, and fed, and given every kindness.
Parents and guardians need not attend. Their names have been taken.
Any person who hinders the carts of this Office in the doing of this kindness will be held to account.
Sweets will be given.
And at the bottom, in ink, in a small round pretty hand that leaned a little to the right, a signature.
A. Pallister. Under-Secretary.
And under the signature, smaller, in a different hand, a hand that did not lean at all, two words.
Seen. Approved.
And beside those two words, very small, pressed so hard into the paper that the wax had spread out round it and blurred, a second seal. Not blue. Gray. Corin turned the paper to the light from the grating and looked at it for a long time. He could not make it out. It was a round seal, and there was something in the middle of it, something with lines going out from it, like the sun in a child's drawing. Or like a crack in ice. He could not tell. The wax had been pressed too hard.
He read the whole notice through twice. Then he gave it back.
"Fifty-one," he said.
"Fifty-one." Silas took off his spectacles and rubbed his eyes with his finger and thumb, very hard. "They counted. They've been counting all week, Vane. They've been in. Somebody has been in, and stood at the bottom of those steps, and counted my children on their pallets, and written them down." He put the spectacles back on. "I thought it was fifty-two. It was fifty-two. Until Ned."
Corin said nothing.
Ned had been ten. Bet's brother. He had died on the Monday, before the sixth bell, on a pallet in the long hall. He had forgotten how to swallow. His coffin was still in the next vault, waiting for the ground to soften enough to dig. Bet had put a tin soldier on the lid.
"The seventh bell," said Silas. "On Midwinter morning. Before the bells. When every family in the river parishes is in church, or in the gin shops, or asleep. When there's nobody on the streets but the Watch." He laughed. It was not a real laugh. "Every kindness."
"What is it?" said Corin quietly. "The House of Rest. You said you went. You asked at the gate."
"Four times. I asked for three of mine. Peg Rudd. Mr. Dobbs. A boy called Lamb, who couldn't remember his first name." Silas's mouth went thin. "Each time a nice man in a brown coat came out to the gate and gave me a peppermint and told me they were very comfortable. Each time I asked to see them. Each time I was told it was not visiting day. It is never visiting day, Vane. Not once, since the autumn."
"And the cart."
"The Friday cart leaves that gate before dawn. I've watched it. Twice. It goes to Cinder Lane. To the coal chute behind the Bourse." He looked at Corin over the crooked spectacles. "You know where it goes after that. You've been there. You've seen the shelf."
Corin had seen the shelf.
Shelf Forty. A whitewashed room, low and long, full of glass jars on wooden racks, and every jar full of a soft gray light that moved a little, like smoke, when you came near. The cold that was taken out of children. Their quiet. Their slow gray falling. Blended, upstairs, into little vials of kindness for the ladies of the Hill to put in their tea. And sold, by the crate, out of the wet door at the back, on the high tide, to men from the north who wanted children's clean cold for the miners. He is the best farmer we have, somebody had said, in that room, about the man with the peppermints.
He looked out of the arch into the long hall.
He could see the nearest pallets from here. Gray blankets, gray faces. A girl of six with her eyes open, watching the lamp. Polly. She had blinked on Thursday, and looked at Lyra, and it had been the best thing that had happened in the crypt all week. Next to her, a small boy curled up with a wooden spoon in his fist. Kit Flynn. Nine. He had stolen apples off a barrow in the autumn and the man who caught him had been a man in a brown coat, and that was how Kit had come to the Fish Stairs, and to the sweets. He did not let go of the spoon, ever. Mrs. Doyle had tried to take it to wash it and he had screamed. Further down there were others. Corin did not know all their names. Silas knew all their names. Silas knew all fifty-one.
"How many can walk?" he said.
"Walk?" Silas looked at him. "Walk where?"
"Anywhere. Out of here."
"Eleven," said Silas at once. He did not have to think. "Eleven, if you hold their hands and go slowly and don't mind them stopping. Another nine if you carry them part of the way. The rest—" He shook his head. "The rest don't know they have legs, Vane. They don't know they're hungry. Half of them don't know their names. You'd have to carry every one. In the snow. On Midwinter Eve. With Harlan Vance's drum boys poking every cart in the city with twelve-foot hooks, and a boy in a gray cap sitting in the graveyard writing down everybody who comes in or out of that door." He took a breath. "And carry them where? Where, Vane? Fifty-one children who are falling. Who need feeding with a spoon, and turning in the night, and washing. Who's going to take them? The arches are gone. Gant cleared the arches out on Wednesday. Mother Grue's people are on the Saltmarsh round Lascar Mary's fire, and they can hardly feed themselves."
"I know."
"Then what—"
"I don't know yet," said Corin.
Silas stopped.
He stood there in the middle of the vault, tall and thin and tired, with the snow melting on his shoulders, and looked down at Corin on the bench. Then he sat down, suddenly, on Oren's empty crate by the bench, as if his long legs had given up on their own. He put his elbows on his knees and his face in his hands.
"I won't let them go," he said through his fingers. "I told you that on Friday. I meant it. I don't care what it costs me. I won't let them go."
"I know you won't."
"They'll take me first. You know that, don't you? Before Monday. That's what under review means. I've written four letters to that man. Four. And every one of them is on his desk. You saw that. He told me himself, at the Fish Stairs, looking at your barrow. Your four letters are on my desk, Doctor. Smiling." Silas lifted his face. "He was smiling, Vane."
"He smiles at everything."
"Yes." Silas looked at the paper in his hand. At the round pretty signature. At the two flat words under it. Seen. Approved. At the gray seal that could not be read. "Who is that?" he said. "Who sees? Who approves? I've been to his office. I've been to the Health. I went up those white steps and in at that door with the hand on the knocker and sat in his warm room with his gold clock and his bowl of white sweets. I thought he was the top of it. I thought, there, that's the man. If I can make him listen, it stops." He put one long finger on the gray seal. "But he isn't the top of it. Is he? Somebody above him reads these. Somebody above him says yes."
Corin looked at the seal too.
He thought of Remy, in the arches, on Tuesday. Remy with his gloves off and his scarred thumbs, talking about the man with the ring. A ring with a dome on it. And rays. Everyone on the Hill knows who wears that ring. They can't remember that they know.
He thought of the words in his Ledger, in his own hand, from the autumn, from the first week, from the night he found out that his own account at the Ministry was sealed. Sealed with the Archon's private seal. He had never seen that seal. He did not know what it looked like.
He did not say any of it.
"Then we find out who," he said instead. "Before Monday. Who reads his papers. Who says yes. Where he takes them." He looked at Silas. "Every order has a road, Doctor. It goes up from one desk to another, and it comes back down signed. If you can't stop the carts, you stop the paper."
"How?"
"I don't know that either." Corin put his gray hand flat on the Ledger. "But I know where he is. He's on the Hill. And it's Saturday. And Saturday is the one day I haven't watched him."
Silas stared at him.
Then he looked down, slowly, at the long straight leg on the bench, in its two splints of ash wood. And back up at Corin's face.
"You," he said. "Are not going up the Hill."
"No?"
"You can't walk to the end of this vault, Vane. You can't get up those steps outside without two people holding you. If you put weight on that leg before the bone has—"
"The knee's gone already," said Corin. "You told me. On Wednesday. It's set. It's not going to get any worse than gone."
"It can get infected. Again. And then I take the leg. And then you die anyway, in a fever, on this bench, and I bury you next to Ned."
"Then don't let it get infected."
Silas opened his mouth. He shut it again. He looked as if he might shout. Corin had never heard him shout. Then he took off his spectacles again and held them in his long fingers and looked at them, as if the answer might be written on the lenses.
"You're as bad as I am," he said at last, very low.
"Worse," said Corin. "I've got less to lose."
And from the floor at the end of the vault, under the grating, a girl's voice said, quite clearly and not at all sleepily:
"That isn't true. And you know it isn't."
Lyra was awake.
